Yesterday we learned that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed alleging that the face recognition feature in Apple Photos violates state privacy laws.

Although the practices of the two companies sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, this case has continually been conflated with Meta's use of face recognition. In allowing the case to proceed, the court fundamentally misunderstands how the feature works……

Earlier allegations against Meta

To properly understand this situation, we need to start with a face recognition lawsuit against Meta dating back to 2015.

Because that face recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify those faces, the company did indeed break the law, and rightly was forced to settle the case for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under that same Illinois law—the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)—which says companies cannot collect biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is fundamentally different

There's one huge problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely did not collect biometric data to perform face recognition in the Apple Photos app. As Apple pointed out in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithms run entirely on-device.

What's more, all the iPhone does is tell you "these photos all look like they might be the same person"—it has no idea who that person is. The only party that can put a name to those faces is the iPhone user themselves.

Apple's Photos privacy policy reflects this as well.

What astounds me is that this lawsuit has been allowed to run for six years in the legal system when a few minutes of research would have shown that the allegations in the lawsuit are clearly wrong.

The courts and legislators should be applauding Apple's privacy-protective approach, not conflating it with privacy-invasive practices from companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of the courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example of this, of course, involves end-to-end encryption—multiple countries have threatened or tried to ban end-to-end encryption without any understanding of how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians can't be experts in every area they need to deal with. But they have access to experts, and what astounds me is that these lawsuits and draft bills can get this far without anyone pointing out these fundamental flaws.
